corpusNote: Anaximander is generally credited with the first work of philosophical prose in the Greek tradition, and with the first surviving verbatim sentence of Western philosophy (DK 12 B1). The Suda lists four titles, but these are almost certainly Alexandrian librarians' headings for sections of a single book rather than four separate works — Anaximander's book, like other early prose works, probably had no title at all, and 'On Nature' is a later convention applied to the whole Presocratic genre.

referenceSystems.name: Diels–Kranz
referenceSystems.note: Anaximander = DK 12. A = testimonia, B = verbatim. B1 is the sole substantial quotation.

works.title: On Nature

date.note: Apollodorus (in DL II.2) dates Anaximander's 64th year to the second year of the 58th Olympiad = 547/546 BCE, and says he died shortly after — a date apparently derived from the book itself.

works.extent: Lost apart from one quoted sentence (DK 12 B1) of roughly 25 words, plus a doxographic reconstruction of the whole in DK 12 A. The single fragment is preserved by Simplicius, Commentary on Aristotle's Physics 24.13–21, quoting Theophrastus.
works.transmission: The chain is: Anaximander → Theophrastus, Opinions of the Natural Philosophers (late 4th c. BCE) → the doxographic tradition → Simplicius (6th c. CE), who quotes Theophrastus quoting Anaximander. Simplicius' remark that Anaximander speaks 'in rather poetical terms' is our warrant that he had actual words in front of him. Where exactly the quotation begins is contested — whether Theophrastus' paraphrase shades into Anaximander's own words at 'according to necessity' or earlier.
works.authenticity: Genuine. The book's existence is not in doubt; what is disputed is its extent, its arrangement, and the precise boundaries of B1 within Simplicius' sentence.
works.summary: The archē is the apeiron — the boundless, unlimited, or indefinite: not one of the elements but that from which they are separated out. The famous fragment: things pass away into those things out of which they have their coming-to-be, 'according to necessity; for they render justice and reparation to one another for their injustice, according to the ordering of time.' The book also carried the cosmogony (the ring-cosmology of fire enclosed in mist, with the heavenly bodies as apertures in wheels), the earth held at the centre unsupported by anything and staying put through equilibrium — an argument Aristotle preserves — and a zoogony in which the first humans developed inside fish-like creatures.
editions: Diels–Kranz, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed. (1951), vol. I, ch. 12
Laks & Most, Early Greek Philosophy, Loeb (2016), vol. II
translations: Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers, 2nd ed. (1983), ch. 3
Laks & Most, Loeb (2016) — Greek and English facing
Freeman, Ancilla to the Pre-Socratic Philosophers (1948) — public domain in most jurisdictions
works.notes: DK 12 B1 is the oldest surviving sentence of Western philosophy. Worth teaching alongside the dispute over its boundaries: what counts as 'the fragment' is itself an editorial decision, visible in the differences between Diels, Kahn, and Conche.

works.title: Circuit of the Earth
works.extent: Lost. Title only, from the Suda.
works.transmission: The title comes from the Suda's list. Independently, Agathemerus and Strabo (citing Eratosthenes) credit Anaximander with being the first to draw a map of the inhabited world — so a geographical work of some kind is well supported even if this title is a librarian's invention.
works.authenticity: Attributed. Most likely a section of the single book rather than a separate publication, or the text accompanying the map.
works.summary: A description of the inhabited world, presumably the written companion to the first Greek world-map. Hecataeus of Miletus later produced a work of the same title, and the tradition may have retrojected it onto Anaximander.
works.notes: The map itself is Anaximander's most consequential production and is not a text: a circular earth, encircled by ocean, with Europe and Asia in symmetrical halves.

works.title: On the Fixed Stars
works.extent: Lost. Title only, from the Suda.
works.authenticity: Attributed. Almost certainly a heading for the astronomical portion of the one book.
works.summary: Presumably the ring-cosmology: sun, moon and stars as fire seen through vents in vast wheels of compressed mist encircling the earth, with the sun's wheel 27 or 28 times the earth's size — the first attempt in Greek to state the cosmos in ratios.
works.notes: The title is suspicious on its own terms: the technical distinction between 'fixed' stars and planets belongs to a much later astronomy than Anaximander's.

works.title: Sphere (Celestial Globe)
works.genre: uncertain — treatise or description of an instrument
works.extent: Lost. Title only, from the Suda.
citations: DL II.2 (on the gnomon and the sphere)
works.transmission: Suda list; Diogenes Laertius II.1–2 credits Anaximander with constructing a sphere and with introducing the gnomon at Sparta to mark solstices and equinoxes.
works.authenticity: Attributed, and ambiguous in kind. The 'Sphere' may be an object he built rather than a book he wrote — the Suda may have converted an artefact into a title.
works.summary: Either a model of the heavens or the text describing one.
works.notes: Good teaching case for how a doxographer's list can silently turn instruments into books.

works.title: Testimonia (DK 12 A)
works.extent: About 30 testimonia in DK 12 A; the substance of what can be known about the system.
works.transmission: Aristotle (on the apeiron and on the earth's equilibrium), then Theophrastus, then the doxographers: Aëtius, Hippolytus, Pseudo-Plutarch, Simplicius, Diogenes Laertius.
works.authenticity: Not by Anaximander; the standard scholarly base for reconstructing him.
works.summary: Includes Aristotle's report of the equilibrium argument for why the earth stays put — that a thing at the centre with no more reason to move one way than another stays where it is — which Karl Popper called one of the boldest arguments in the history of thought.

sources: Diels–Kranz, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, ch. 12
Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers, 2nd ed.
